notes.body:
The apparent contradiction dissolves when we notice that the author is pointing to two angles of a single movement of the soul. Intense love (عِشْق) is one — the consuming love that pulls a seeker toward the Beloved with every breath, leaving no room in the heart for anything else. Direct spiritual tasting (ذَوْق) is the other: **the moment of unmediated encounter**, like the tongue touching sweetness before the mind has any word for it.

When the author first says عِشْق is "another name for the fervent longing... which is ذَوْق," he is not declaring them identical. He is saying they occupy the same ineffable register — and anyone who has experienced one is already moving inside the territory of the other. When he separates them as "Love and ذَوْق," he acknowledges there is still **a distinction worth naming**. عِشْق is the state of the seeker — the burning that makes a person reach. ذَوْق is the state of the encounter — the direct experience of what was sought.

Think of someone whose love for music is so intense that the first note of a beloved piece brings them to tears — that is عِشْق. The sensation of the sound landing, that moment of direct experience, is ذَوْق. Yet **neither can exist without the other**, and neither can be explained to someone who has never heard music — which is why the author insists both are beyond speech and writing.

So عِشْق and ذَوْق are not two ranked stations on a ladder. They are **two faces of a single spiritual reality** — the orientation of the heart and its confirmation.

etymology: عِشْق (intense love): root ع-ش-ق. The root conjures the عَاشِقَة — a clinging vine that fastens so tightly around whatever it grips that it cannot be pulled away. From this image comes عِشْق: love so total the lover clings entirely to the Beloved, unable to detach. Not ordinary affection, but the consuming attachment that leaves no space in the heart for anything else.

ذَوْق (tasting, direct experience): root ذ-و-ق. From ذَاقَ, to taste — originally taking a small portion to know its quality by direct contact with the tongue. The Quran uses ذَآئِقَة in "every soul shall taste death" (Al-Imran 3:185), carrying the same quality of immediate, undeniable encounter. Spiritually, ذَوْق is the direct experience of a reality that cannot be transmitted to one who has not themselves tasted.

notes.body:
The hadith looks, at first, like a simple formula for dividing our time and energy. But Shibli saw something deeper. **The principle it contains is honest proportion** — and when applied with full sincerity, it does not balance four competing claims; it reveals that three of them are almost nothing.

Consider the arithmetic the hadith forces upon us. How long will we live in this world? A few decades, perhaps. How long in the hereafter? Without end. So the effort we owe this world is a fraction of a fraction, and the effort we owe the hereafter is everything. Then comes the sharpest question: how much do we need Allah? Entirely. Without Him, nothing we are or have or do holds together for a single moment. And how much pain of the Fire can we bear? None. Followed faithfully, the hadith's arithmetic collapses into a single direction: give everything toward Allah and what He has prescribed, and give this world only as much as it genuinely requires.

This is why Shibli could say he found in it the knowledge of all who came first and all who came last. Every prophet, every teacher, every tradition of guidance has ultimately been saying the same thing: **know your real situation, and let that knowledge govern your effort**. The Prophet (ع) himself sought refuge from knowledge that bears no fruit in action, because knowledge that does not reshape how we live is accumulation without transformation.

The passage connects this directly to مُجَاهَدَة, the disciplined inner struggle, because the proportional vision the hadith demands is itself that struggle. To sit quietly and reckon honestly — how long am I here, how long is forever, how much do I need Him — and then to let that reckoning cut away the excess, is exactly what مُجَاهَدَة looks like in practice. Shibli's single hadith was not a shortcut; **it was the one key that unlocks every door**.

notes.quote: I found in this one hadith the knowledge of all who came first and all who came last
etymology: قَدْر (measure, proportion): from the root ق-د-ر, meaning to measure, to decree, to be capable. The same root gives قَدَر (divine decree) and قُدْرَة (power, ability). In the hadith, بِقَدْرِ means 'in proportion to' — the word carries the sense that true measure is already written into the nature of a thing, and our effort must align with that reality.

مُجَاهَدَة (disciplined inner struggle): from the root ج-ه-د, meaning to exert, to strive, to push to one's limit. The same root gives جِهَاد and اِجْتِهَاد (independent reasoning by effort). The form مُفَاعَلَة implies a sustained, ongoing engagement — مُجَاهَدَة is not a single push but a continuing discipline, a daily wrestling with the demands of the lower self.
